name: Francis Howard Williams
bio: Francis Howard Williams (1844–1922) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Philadelphia, where he worked for a trust company and contributed to various journals.
He wrote the lyric drama The Princess Elizabeth (1880) and several comedies and pastorals. Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poems.title: Electra
poems.author: Francis Howard Williams
poems.collection: An American Anthology, 1787–1900, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900)
poems.text:
My Love too stately is to be but fair,
Too fair she is for naught but stateliness;
She bids me Nay, and yet a silent Yes
Dwells in the dusk her shadowy eyelids wear.
My Love’s step makes a music in the air,
Touching the sense with a divine caress,
And all the rapture of the dawn doth bless
The light that leaps to life across her hair.
Her mouth is just the love-couch for a song,
And mid the fragrance of its riven flowers
Low laughter breaks and trembles close to tears
Mingled of mirth and melody, as a throng
Of bird notes wakes to joy the drowsy hours
And weaves delight through all the grieving years.

poems.title: Walt Whitman
poems.author: Francis Howard Williams
poems.collection: An American Anthology, 1787–1900, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900)
poems.text:
Darkness and death? Nay, Pioneer, for thee
The day of deeper vision has begun;
There is no darkness for the central sun
Nor any death for immortality.
At last the song of all fair songs that be,
At last the guerdon of a race well run,
The upswelling joy to know the victory won,
The river’s rapture when it finds the sea.
Ah, thou art wrought in an heroic mould,
The modern man upon whose brow yet stays
A gleam of glory from the age of gold,—
A diadem which all the gods have kissed.
Hail and farewell! flower of the antique days,—
Democracy’s divine protagonist.

poems.title: Song
poems.author: Francis Howard Williams
poems.collection: An American Anthology, 1787–1900, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900)
poems.text:
A bird in my bower
    Sat calling, a-calling;
A bird answered low from the garden afar.
  His note came with power,
    While falling, a-falling,
Her note quivered faint as the light of a star.
  “I am Life! I am Life!”
    From the bower a-ringing,
Trilled forth a mad melody, soaring above;
  “I am Love! I am Love!”
    From the garden a-singing,
Came soft as a dream, and the echoes sang “Love.”

  They joined, and together
    Fast flying, a-flying,
Were lost to my gaze in the arch of the sky.
  The wind through the heather
    Is sighing, a-sighing;
Ah! how should it ever do other than sigh?
  Where art thou, where art thou,
    Life, flying, a-flying?
Where art thou, O Love, sweetest child of the dawn?
  The song in the meadow
    Is dying, a-dying;
My heart groweth heavy, and whispereth—“Gone.”
